text.p: The European Commission said on Friday that inflation across the 15-nation European Union was 2.2 percent in January compared with a year earlier, using a new harmonised method of calculation.

The harmonised indices, which will be used next year for deciding which countries qualify for the single currency, showed some countries with significantly different rates than previously published by national statistics agencies.

For example, Sweden's harmonised inflation figure amounted to 1.3 percent compared with the nationally published figure of a fall of 0.1 percent and Britain's harmonised rise was 2.1 percent compared with the increase of 2.8 percent reported nationally.

The harmonised data, worked out in cooperation between the EU's statistics agency and national statistics offices, showed that Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg had the bloc's lowest inflation rates in January -- 0.9 percent, 1.3 percent and 1.3 percent respectively.
Greece, Portugal and Spain had the highest rates -- 6.6 percent, 2.8 percent and 2.8 percent respectively.

According to the EU's Maastricht treaty, a country's average inflation rate observed over a year before joining EMU should "not exceed by more than 1.5 percentage points that of, at most, the three best performing member states in terms of price stability". -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
